Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

Because the narrative spans several years—covering Denise and Daniel's meeting, an eleven-month courtship, the early stages of their marriage, and the three years it takes to build their business—the author effectively uses summary and exposition to compress time and provide necessary background (such as Miss Emily's business history and Denise's eleven years at the grocery store). However, the emotional core and turning points of the story are always grounded in vivid, real-time scenes with sharp dialogue, such as Daniel buying the single shallot, the first dinner with Miss Emily, the late-night kitchen scene where Denise fixes the velouté recipe, and the negotiation of the business loan. This seamless alternation allows the story to maintain an engaging pace while still feeling intimate and dramatized.
